subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: What are biological databases? Give their classification
subjective.answer: Biological databases in general store biological data, and their main goals are: (1) data storage, (2) information retrieval, and (3) knowledge discovery. Classification: biological databases can be classified as: • Primary databases (which store the primary sequences) • Secondary databases (the primary sequences are annotated and kept in secondary databases) • Specialized databases (dedicated to some specific organism, or containing data about some disease) Biological databases can also be classified on the basis of the type of data they contain, such as nucleotide databases, protein databases, RNA databases, genome databases and expression (gene expression) databases.

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: What is the difference between EMBL and DDBJ?
subjective.answer: • The European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) was established in Europe in 1980. • The DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ) was established in Mishima, Japan, in 1984. GenBank, DDBJ and EMBL joined together in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC). The NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information), DDBJ (DNA Data Bank of Japan) and EBI (European Bioinformatics Institute) / ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) form this international collaboration (INSDC). EMBL established EBI to deal with bioinformatics work, and within it ENA was established to maintain the DNA sequence datasets.

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: Write a note on the SWISS-PROT, FASTA and GenBank sequence formats.
subjective.answer: SWISS-PROT is an annotated protein sequence database established in 1986 and maintained collaboratively, since 1987, by the Department of Medical Biochemistry of the University of Geneva and the EMBL Data Library (now the EMBL Outstation — the European Bioinformatics Institute). FASTA sequence format: DNA sequences are stored in specified formats, and different software needs sequences in different formats. FASTA is the most frequently used format to present DNA and protein sequences. It is recommended that all lines of text be shorter than 80 characters in length. Example: >gi|568815581:c7687550-7668402 Homo sapiens chromosome 17, GRCh38 Primary Assembly GATGGGATTGGGGTTTTCCCCTCCCATGTGCTCATCTAGAGCCACCGTCCAGGGAGCAGGTAGCTG CTGGGCTCTCCACGACGGTGACACGC-------- GenBank format: a sequence file in GenBank format can contain several sequences. One sequence starts with a line containing the word LOCUS and a number of annotation lines. The start of the sequence is marked by a line containing "ORIGIN" and the end of the sequence is marked by two slashes ("//").

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: What is the difference between the GenBank format and the FASTA format?
subjective.answer: GenBank to FASTA accepts a GenBank file as input and returns the entire DNA sequence in FASTA format. Use this program when you wish to quickly remove all of the non-DNA sequence information from a GenBank file: paste the contents of one or more GenBank files into the text area. (In other words, a GenBank file carries the sequence together with its annotation lines, while FASTA keeps only a description line beginning with ">" followed by the sequence itself.)

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: Write a note on SWISS-PROT
subjective.answer: SWISS-PROT is a curated protein sequence database which strives to provide a high level of annotation (such as the description of the function of a protein, its domain structure, post-translational modifications, variants, etc.), a minimal level of redundancy and a high level of integration with other databases. Recent developments of the database include format and content enhancements, cross-references to additional databases, new documentation files and improvements to TrEMBL, a computer-annotated supplement to SWISS-PROT. TrEMBL consists of entries in SWISS-PROT-like format derived from the translation of all coding sequences (CDSs) in the EMBL Nucleotide Sequence Database, except the CDSs already included in SWISS-PROT. The Human Proteomics Initiative (HPI), a major project to annotate all known human sequences according to the quality standards of SWISS-PROT, is also described. SWISS-PROT is available at http://www.expasy.ch/sprot/ and http://www.ebi.ac.uk/swissprot/

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: What is the XML format (for sequence data)?
subjective.answer: XML is a modern practice in which we try to put sequences in a kind of machine language. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language. The format is similar to HTML (the language for web programming). The good part is that this language is in between machine-readable and man-readable, so it is kind of easy to code over this, and it is becoming a standard data format for transferring genome data. Example (XML Schema for the SBOL core data model): <xsd:annotation> <xsd:documentation> XML Schema for SBOL core data model compatible with RDF/XML serialization. <dc:date>2012-01-19</dc:date> <dc:creator>Evren Sirin</dc:creator> <dc:contributor>Michal Galdzicki</dc:contributor> </xsd:documentation> </xsd:annotation>

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: Why are sequences submitted to databases? What precautions should be taken when submitting a sequence?
subjective.answer: Sequences are submitted to the databases in order to share them with the scientific community. Generally, sequences are submitted at the time of publication and are reviewed by peers. Caution: It is important to ensure that sequence files do not contain any special characters. Control characters in addition to standard ASCII characters must be removed, else they might mess up the analysis or data transfer.

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: What is GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus)? What kinds of records does it have?
subjective.answer: GEO is a public repository for the archiving and distribution of gene expression data submitted by the scientific community. It is MIAME compliant (Minimum Information About a Microarray Experiment). It is convenient for deposition of gene expression data, as required by funding agencies and journals. It is a curated resource for gene expression data, with browsing, querying, analysis and retrieval. GEO has four kinds of records: • Sample (GSM) — preparation and description of the samples • Platform (GPL) — technology used and the features detected (microarray or RNA-Seq) • Series (GSE) — defines a set of samples and how they are related • Datasets (GDS) — sample data collections assembled by GEO

subjective.topic: Biological Databases and Sequence Formats
subjective.question: What are primary medical databases? Enlist four medical databases.
subjective.answer: Primary medical databases store medical and health-care data. An example is the NIVEL Primary Care Database: it collects data that is routinely recorded in the health care provider's electronic health record system. This includes data on health problems and treatment. Well-known medical / health databases include PubMed / MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: What is the KMP Matcher (Knuth–Morris–Pratt algorithm)?
subjective.answer: Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) is an algorithm which checks the characters from left to right. When a pattern has a sub-pattern that appears more than once in the sub-pattern, it uses that property to improve the time complexity, also in the worst case. The time complexity of KMP is O(n). It is a linear-time algorithm for string matching and does not involve backtracking on the string S (i.e., no repetitive comparison of nucleotide residues). Its components are: • The Prefix Function Π: it encapsulates knowledge about how the pattern matches against shifts of itself. This information can be used to avoid useless shifts of the pattern 'p', which enables avoiding backtracking on the string 'S'. • The KMP Matcher: Given the string 'S', pattern 'p' and prefix function 'Π', it finds the occurrence of 'p' in 'S' and returns the number of shifts of 'p' after which the occurrence is found.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: Write the generalized algorithm for pattern finding.
subjective.answer: Goal: Find all occurrences of a pattern in text. Input: Pattern p = [p1…pn] of length n; Text t = [t1…tm] of length m. Output: An indication that pattern P exists in T, or it does not exist in T.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: What are the four cases of pattern finding?
subjective.answer: Pattern recognition is the automated recognition of patterns and regularities in data. Pattern recognition is closely related to artificial intelligence and machine learning, together with applications such as data mining and knowledge discovery in databases (KDD), and is often used interchangeably with these terms. However, these are distinguished: machine learning is one approach to pattern recognition, while other approaches include hand-crafted (not learned) rules or heuristics; and pattern recognition is one approach to artificial intelligence, while other approaches include symbolic artificial intelligence.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: List the methods of finding patterns in a genome.
subjective.answer: • Exact searching method • Approximate searching method • Position weight matrices • Suffix tree

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: What is a suffix tree?
subjective.answer: A suffix tree is a compressed tree containing all the suffixes of a string, and it allows many problems on strings to be solved quickly. String problems are solved by: exact searching or pattern matching methods; approximate searching or pattern matching methods; position weight matrices; and suffix trees.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: What is the Bypass algorithm (branch and bound)?
subjective.answer: The Bypass algorithm works with the Branch and Bound algorithm and the NextVertex algorithm: it skips the subtree rooted at vertex (a, i) and increments ai (unless ai = k). In the search tree, the numbers next to a leaf represent the "score" for that L-mer, and scores at internal vertices represent the maximum score in the subtree rooted at that vertex. To improve the brute force algorithm, we can "prune" subtrees that do not contain high-scoring leaves. For example, since the score of the very first leaf is 24, it does not make sense to analyze the 4th, 5th or 6th leaves whose scores are 20, 4 and 5 respectively; therefore, the subtree containing these vertices can be ignored.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: Describe the brute force algorithm for the Partial Digest Problem.
subjective.answer: • Take the largest distance in "L". • These are the outermost points of "X". • The remaining distance is "δ". Example: L = {2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10}. The size of L is n(n−1)/2 = 10, where n is the number of points in the solution. Here n is 5, and the positions of X are x1 = 0, x2, x3, x4 and x5.

subjective.topic: Pattern Matching and String Algorithms
subjective.question: What is the Partial Digest Problem?
subjective.answer: Partial Digest Problem: Given all pairwise distances between points on a line, reconstruct the positions of those points. Input: The multiset of pairwise distances L, containing n(n−1)/2 integers. Output: A set X of n integers such that ∆X = L. ∆A is equal to ∆(A ⊕ {v}), where A ⊕ {v} is defined to be {a + v : a ∈ A}. Also ∆A = ∆(−A), where −A = {−a : a ∈ A}. Example: A = {0, 2, 4, 7, 10}; ∆(A ⊕ {100}) = {100, 102, 104, 107, 110}, and −A = {−10, −7, −4, −2, 0}. Two sets giving the same distances: {0, 1, 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15} and {0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 12, 13, 15}.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: Define the Local Alignment Problem (its input and output)
subjective.answer: Local Alignment Problem: Find the best local alignment between two strings. Input: Strings v and w and a scoring matrix δ. Output: Substrings of v and w whose global alignment, as defined by δ, is maximal among all global alignments of all substrings of v and w.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What is the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem?
subjective.answer: The simplest form of a sequence similarity analysis is the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem, where we eliminate the operation of substitution and allow only insertions and deletions. A subsequence of a string v is simply an (ordered) sequence of characters (not necessarily consecutive) from v.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What is an alignment? How is an alignment score calculated?
subjective.answer: An alignment is the arrangement of two sequences one above the other so that matching residues are placed in the same columns, with gaps (spaces) introduced where insertions or deletions occurred. The "alignment score" is the "matching score" used in the definition of sequence identity: the score of an alignment is computed by adding the scores of the aligned residue pairs (from the scoring matrix) and subtracting the penalties for gaps. Indels: the columns of the alignment containing one space are called indels, with the columns containing a space in the top row called insertions and the columns with a space in the bottom row called deletions.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What is edit distance? Explain with an example.
subjective.answer: Edit distance between two strings is the minimum number of editing operations needed to transform one string into another, where the edit operations are insertion, deletion, and substitution of one symbol for another. It is often the case that the ith symbol in one sequence corresponds to a symbol at a different position in the other. Mutations in DNA are an evolutionary process: DNA replication — substitutions, insertions, and deletions of nucleotides — leads to "edited" DNA texts, so edit distance measures how many such changes separate two sequences.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What is an edit graph?
subjective.answer: The grid that is achieved after alignment is similar to the Manhattan grid, where each entry in the grid looks like a city block. This graph is called the Edit Graph. The main difference between the Manhattan grid and the Edit Graph is that we can also move along the diagonals in the Edit Graph.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What are the types of complexity (in algorithm analysis)?
subjective.answer: Three types of complexity could be considered when analyzing algorithm performance: worst-case complexity, best-case complexity, and average-case complexity. The average-case running time, for a function f(n) where a, b and c are constants, can be described as an average between the best-case and worst-case.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What is the (brute force) runtime of an algorithm?
subjective.answer: In actual cases, the performance (runtime) of an algorithm depends on n, that is, the size of the input or the number of operations required for each input item. For a brute force algorithm the runtime grows quicker than the previous (polynomial) algorithms based on n — it grows even faster than a polynomial algorithm.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What is gene prediction (gene finding)?
subjective.answer: In computational biology, gene prediction or gene finding refers to the process of identifying the regions of genomic DNA that encode genes. This includes protein-coding genes as well as RNA genes, but may also include prediction of other functional elements such as regulatory regions.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What is the Exon Chaining problem?
subjective.answer: In the Exon Chaining problem, the weight of the path is defined as the optimal alignment score between the concatenated labels (blocks) and the target sequence. Exon Chaining assumes the positions and weights of exons are pre-defined. Example: Five weighted intervals, (2, 3, 3), (4, 8, 6), (9, 10, 1), (11, 15, 7) and (16, 18, 4), shown by bold edges, form an optimal solution to the Exon Chaining problem. The array at the bottom shows the values s1, s2, …, s2n generated by the EXONCHAINING algorithm.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What is exon prediction? Name a tool used for it.
subjective.answer: GeneAlign is a coding exon prediction tool for predicting protein coding genes by measuring the homologies between a sequence of a genome and related sequences, which have been annotated, of other genomes. The rates of missing exons and wrong exons are smaller than 1%.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: Describe the similarity-based approach of gene prediction.
subjective.answer: A similarity-based approach works with previously sequenced genes to find unknown genes in newly sequenced DNA fragments. It is a combinatorial puzzle: find a set of substrings (candidate exons) whose splicing best fits the target. The brute force approach finds all local similarities: each substring from the genomic sequence that exhibits sufficient similarity to the target protein could be considered a putative exon, with exon-flanking dinucleotides AG and GT, and overlapping candidates. A putative exon is modelled with a weighted interval in the genomic sequence, with parameters (l, r, w): l is the left-hand position, r is the right-hand position, and w is the weight of the putative exon — the local alignment score, i.e., the likelihood that this interval is an exon. A chain is any set of non-overlapping weighted intervals; the aim is a maximum-weight chain, and weights of all intervals are positive (w > 0).

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What are the steps of genome annotation?
subjective.answer: Genome annotation is an important first step in genome analysis, based on finding significant alignment to sequences of known function in databases. There are two steps in genome annotation: • Structural annotation • Functional annotation

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What is structural annotation? What can we do by using this technique?
subjective.answer: Structural annotation is the identification of gene features like: • Promoters • Terminators • Shine-Dalgarno sites • DNA motifs • Co-transcription units • Operons in microbes MAGPIE (Multipurpose Automated Genome Project Investigation Environment) is an automated genome analysis tool that is used for structural annotation. Structural annotations are physical regions of a genome that encode a genomic feature. Examples of such annotations are genes, mRNA, transcripts and repeat sequences.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What are GeneQuiz and MAGPIE?
subjective.answer: MAGPIE (Multipurpose Automated Genome Project Investigation Environment) is an automated genome analysis tool that is used for structural annotation. GeneQuiz focuses on deriving a predicted protein function based upon available evidence, including evaluation of similarity to the closest homologue in the database.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: Write a note on ORF (Open Reading Frame).
subjective.answer: An open reading frame (ORF) is the part of a reading frame that has the potential to be translated. Consider a genome of length n as a sequence of n/3 codons. There are three stop codons (TAA, TAG and TGA); the sub-segments that start from a start codon, ATG, are ORFs. An ORF is a continuous stretch of codons that contains a start codon (usually AUG) and a stop codon (usually UAA, UAG or UGA). An ATG codon within the ORF (not necessarily the first) may indicate where translation starts. The transcription termination site is located after the ORF, beyond the translation stop codon; if transcription were to cease before the stop codon, an incomplete protein would be made during translation. ORFs within a single genomic sequence may overlap, since there are six possible reading frames: three on one strand starting at positions 1, 2 and 3, and three on the reverse strand. In eukaryotic genes with multiple exons, ORFs span intron/exon regions, which may be spliced together after transcription of the ORF to yield the final mRNA for protein translation.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: What are donor site and acceptor splice junctions?
subjective.answer: Donor site: Coding region | GT (the intron starts with GT). Acceptor site: (the intron ends) YAG | Coding region — where Y can be any pyrimidine.

subjective.topic: Gene Prediction, Exons and Genome Annotation
subjective.question: Write a note on introns, exons and the splicing process.
subjective.answer: Introns: An intron is a long stretch of non-coding DNA found between exons (or coding regions) in a gene. Genes that contain introns are known as discontinuous or split genes, as the coding regions are not continuous. Introns are found only in eukaryotic organisms. Exons: An exon is any part of a gene that will encode a part of the final mature RNA produced by that gene after introns have been removed by RNA splicing. The term exon refers to both the DNA sequence within a gene and to the corresponding sequence in RNA transcripts. Splicing process: RNA splicing is a process that removes introns and joins exons in a primary transcript. An intron usually contains a clear signal for splicing (e.g., the beta globin gene). In some cases (e.g., the Tau gene), a splicing signal may be masked by a regulatory protein, resulting in alternative splicing. A splice site mutation is a genetic mutation that inserts, deletes or changes a number of nucleotides in the specific site at which splicing takes place during the processing of precursor mRNA into mature mRNA. Splice site consensus sequences that drive exon recognition are located at the very termini of introns. Deletion of the splicing site results in one or more introns remaining in mature mRNA and may lead to the production of abnormal proteins.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: Define pseudogenes
subjective.answer: These are non-functional genes. Sometimes there are mutations in the genes, and if those mutations are present in some important regions then the gene's function gets knocked out — such genes are known as pseudogenes. There is one category of them known as processed pseudogenes, which lack introns and promoters. A pseudogene is a DNA sequence that resembles a gene but has been mutated into an inactive form over the course of evolution. It often lacks introns and other essential DNA sequences necessary for function. Though genetically similar to the original functional gene, pseudogenes do not result in functional proteins, although some may have regulatory effects.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: Write a note on mitochondrial DNA and chloroplast DNA
subjective.answer: Mitochondrial DNA (in both animals and plants) and chloroplast DNA (in plants) are found in membrane-bound organelles, and they may be present in hundreds to thousands of copies (so there are also multiple copies of these genomes). The mitochondrion is the site for respiration, whereas the chloroplast is the site for photosynthesis. Their DNAs can be labelled as mtDNA or cpDNA respectively. Plasmids, yeast, transposons, viral genomes and retroviruses are other examples of organellar DNA.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What are tandem repeats and interspersed repeats?
subjective.answer: Tandem repeats occur in DNA when a pattern of one or more nucleotides is repeated and the repetitions are directly adjacent to each other. Several protein domains also form tandem repeats within their amino acid primary structure, such as armadillo repeats. Interspersed repeats are repeated DNA sequences located at dispersed regions in a genome. They are also known as mobile elements or transposable elements: a stretch of DNA sequence may be copied to a different location through DNA recombination. So repeats can be tandem repeats (an array of repeats together) or interspersed repeats (repeats separated by normal genome, i.e., normal genome lies between those repeats). Short Tandem Repeats (STRs): Analyzing STRs is more accurate than the RFLP technique because their small size makes them easier to separate. To create a fingerprint, you might look at 20 different STRs at different places in order to create a profile.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: Write a note on LINEs and SINEs, chromatin and heterochromatin
subjective.answer: • SINEs (Short Interspersed Nuclear Elements) — 80–300 bp long; Alu repeats are an example. • LINEs (Long Interspersed Nuclear Elements) — 6–8 kb long. Chromatin is a mass of genetic material composed of DNA and proteins that condenses to form chromosomes during eukaryotic cell division. Chromatin is located in the nucleus of our cells. Heterochromatin is a tightly packed form of DNA, or condensed DNA, which comes in multiple varieties. These varieties lie on a continuum between the two extremes of constitutive heterochromatin and facultative heterochromatin. Both play a role in the expression of genes.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What are MITEs?
subjective.answer: MITEs (Miniature Inverted-repeat Transposable Elements) have features of both Class I and Class II elements and are about 400 bp in size.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What is a genome? What is genome informatics?
subjective.answer: Genome: Genome sequencing provides the sequences of all the genes of an organism. A major application of bioinformatics is the analysis of full genomes that have been sequenced. The challenge is to identify those genes that are predicted to have a particular biological function. Genome informatics is the field in which computational and statistical techniques are applied to derive biological information from genome sequences. Genome informatics includes methods to analyze DNA sequence information and to predict protein sequence and structure.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What is MS2?
subjective.answer: MS2 infects E. coli and Enterobacteriaceae. It is a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus and encodes the MS2 coat protein. In MS2 sequencing, the entire nucleotide sequence was established by nuclease digestion and characterization. (Its genome is also referred to in the paper's format question: 49 different codons in the genetic code specify the sequence of the 129 amino-acid-long coat polypeptide.)

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What is collinearity of a gene and its protein? Who proved it?
subjective.answer: Charles Yanofsky proved that a gene and its protein product are collinear. Yanofsky's experiment was so influential that nobody even questioned codons, and for almost 2 decades biologists believed that a protein was encoded by a long string of adjacent triplets.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: Describe DNA (the region/structure of DNA).
subjective.answer: The vast majority of organisms encode their genes in long strands of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). DNA consists of a chain made from four types of nucleotide subunits, each composed of: a five-carbon sugar (2-deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and one of the four bases adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What is the difference between DNA and RNA?
subjective.answer: DNA is a double-stranded molecule while RNA is a single-stranded molecule. DNA is stable under alkaline conditions while RNA is not stable. DNA and RNA base pairing is slightly different, since DNA uses the bases adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine, while RNA uses adenine, uracil, cytosine and guanine.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What is translation (of a protein)?
subjective.answer: Protein synthesis is accomplished through a process called translation. After DNA is transcribed into a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule during transcription, the mRNA must be translated to produce a protein. In translation, mRNA along with transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomes work together to produce proteins.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: How can a mutation in DNA be detected/analyzed?
subjective.answer: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can be used to permit rapid analysis of any known mutation in genomic DNA.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What is a restriction enzyme?
subjective.answer: A restriction enzyme is a protein that recognizes a specific, short nucleotide sequence and cuts the DNA only at that specific site, which is known as the restriction site or target sequence. More than 400 restriction enzymes have been isolated from the bacteria that manufacture them.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: Write a detail note on sequence logos.
subjective.answer: A sequence logo is a graphical representation of the sequence conservation of nucleotides (in a strand of DNA/RNA) or amino acids (in protein sequences). A sequence logo is created from a collection of aligned sequences and depicts the consensus sequence and the diversity of the sequences. • It is a visual representation of a position-specific distribution. • It is easy for nucleotides, but we need colour to depict up to 20 amino acid proportions. • The overall height at a position is proportional to the information content. • The proportions of each nucleotide/amino acid are in relation to their observed frequency, with the most frequent on top and the next most frequent below.

subjective.topic: Genes, Genome Structure and Repetitive DNA
subjective.question: What are NF-κB binding sites (in the context of motif finding)?
subjective.answer: NF-κB binding sites (nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells) are regulatory motifs where transcription factors bind. In the motif-finding problem, we are given a set of upstream regions of genes in the genome, each region containing one NF-κB site, and we suppose we do not know either the location or the sequence of the NF-κB sites — the task is to find them.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: What is the difference between mouse synteny and the human X chromosome (synteny between mouse and human)?
subjective.answer: Synteny between species means not only that orthologous genes (identical in functionality and ancestry) are present, but that they are present in the same order on the genome, thus indicating common ancestry. Comparison of the mouse genome sequence with the previously sequenced human genome reveals that 90.2% of the human genome and 93.3% of the mouse genome lie in conserved segments. So not only can we find homologous sequences between the two genomes; the genes also lie on the chromosome in the same order. This is powerful evidence for common ancestry.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: What is synteny? Why is it important? Give an example.
subjective.answer: Synteny means that orthologous genes are present in the same order on the chromosomes of two species. Exceptional conservation of synteny can reflect important functional relationships between genes. Synteny is widely used in studying complex genomes, as comparative genomics allows the presence and possibly the function of genes in a simpler, model organism to infer those in a more complex one. For example, many of the genes of humans are syntenic with those of other mammals — not only apes but also cows, mice and so on. Study of synteny can show how the genome is cut and pasted in the course of evolution.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: Write a note on Waardenburg syndrome.
subjective.answer: Waardenburg syndrome is a group of genetic conditions that can cause hearing loss and changes in coloring (pigmentation) of the hair, skin and eyes. Although most people with Waardenburg syndrome have normal hearing, moderate to profound hearing loss can occur in one or both ears. Its features include hearing loss and two different colored eyes. The gene is present on chromosome 2. The Splotch gene in mice is its counterpart: the human genome and mouse genome can be cut into about 300 genomic fragments (synteny blocks) — chromosome 2 in humans corresponds to mouse chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 14 and 17. Genome rearrangement results in a change of gene ordering; analysis of the human and mouse genomes shows about 250 genomic rearrangements.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: Write a note on the Human Genome Project.
subjective.answer: The pilot project, the Human Genome Initiative, was begun by the Department of Energy (DOE) in 1986. The National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), a federally funded organization (NIH), started in 1988 (Francis Collins). Celera, a commercial vendor (Craig Venter), joined the venture in 1998. Both simultaneously announced the completion of the project in 2000. A total of 3.4 billion bases were sequenced at a cost of $1/base. The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the sequence of nucleotide base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying and mapping all of the genes of the human genome from both a physical and a functional standpoint.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: Name the model organisms used in genome studies
subjective.answer: Most of the time, while doing genome sequencing projects, our objective is to find the cure of some disease, or improve some variety of a crop for enhancing its production, or look into drugs against different organisms — so it is a good idea to have model organisms that can be used for studying various processes in labs. The range of model organisms includes: 1. E. coli — bacteria 2. S. cerevisiae — yeast 3. C. elegans — worm 4. D. melanogaster — fly 5. Danio rerio — zebrafish 6. Mus musculus — mouse 7. Homo sapiens — human 8. Arabidopsis — plant

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: What is self-comparison of a proteome?
subjective.answer: Self-comparison of the proteome is done when we are interested in finding genes which are duplicated within the same organism. The proteome is the collection of the proteins derived from a genome; therefore, the whole collection of one organism's proteins can be termed its proteome, and we can compare it with itself to find out about those sequences which are duplicated in it.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: What is the difference between clustering by subgraph and clustering by linkage?
subjective.answer: Clustering by subgraph: • Each sequence is a vertex • A significant alignment score is an edge • Trimming is done by removing weak edges (high P/E values) Clustering by linkage: • Each sequence is a vertex • A significant alignment score is an edge • Trimming is done by removing weak edges (high P/E), or removing edges above e-6 • The remaining subgraph should share 2/3 of the edges

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: Write the general algorithm for hierarchical agglomerative clustering
subjective.answer: Hierarchical agglomerative general algorithm: • Find the 2 closest objects and merge them into a cluster. • Find and merge the next two closest points, where a point is either an individual object or a cluster of objects. • If more than one cluster remains, return to step 2.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: Write the Preorder (tree traversal) algorithm.
subjective.answer: PREORDER(v) 1. Output v 2. If v has children: 3. PREORDER(left child of v) 4. PREORDER(right child of v)

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: What are Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers? Explain with an example.
subjective.answer: The Enzyme Commission (EC), working under the IUBMB (International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology), proposed that enzymes are classified on the basis of the reactions they catalyze, with a 4-digit scheme — the enzyme commission number: EC a.b.c.d. • 'a' (first digit) informs that it is from one of the 6 classes of biochemical reactions. • 'b' (second digit) informs about the group of substrate (the thing on which the enzyme attacks). • 'c' (third digit) informs about the acceptor molecule. • 'd' (fourth digit) gives the details of the biochemical reaction. Example: tripeptide aminopeptidase, EC 3.4.11.4 — 3 tells us it is a hydrolase (uses water to break the substrate); 3.4 tells us it is a hydrolase that acts on peptide bonds; 3.4.11 tells us it is a hydrolase that cleaves the amino-terminal amino acids of a polypeptide; and EC 3.4.11.4 together tells us it is a hydrolase that cleaves the amino-terminal amino acids of a tripeptide.

subjective.question: What is personalized medicine?
subjective.answer: Personalized medicine, precision medicine, or theranostics, is a medical model that separates people into different groups — with medical decisions, practices, interventions and/or products being tailored to the individual patient based on their predicted response or risk of disease.

subjective.topic: Comparative Genomics, Clustering and Applications
subjective.question: Differentiate proteome and core proteome.
subjective.answer: Proteome: The proteome is the entire set of proteins that is, or can be, expressed by a genome, cell, tissue, or organism at a certain time. It is the set of expressed proteins in a given type of cell or organism, at a given time, under defined conditions. Core proteome: The core proteome is the set of proteins that are common to all the organisms of a group (for example, all strains of a species); it is obtained by comparing the proteomes of different organisms and keeping the proteins they all share.

subjective.topic: Sequence Alignment, Similarity and Algorithm Complexity
subjective.question: What do you mean by highly conserved region in an alignment?
subjective.answer: A highly conserved region in an alignment is a stretch of positions (nucleotides or amino acids) that remains almost identical across the aligned sequences of different organisms. Such regions change very little during evolution because they are functionally important, so harmful mutations in them are removed by natural selection. Highly conserved regions therefore indicate functionally significant parts of a gene or protein, such as active sites and binding sites.
